erText: The 20-mark questions are a major differentiator on this paper. In this series, it was also very evident that those who prepared well gained access to the full range of marks. The best responses evidence a deep and secure knowledge and understanding of the specification area/s being tested. Attention to detail is always strong and case study support is almost always very accurate. Less successful responses tend to fall down for a number of reasons. Students sometimes misread the question or, in the heat of examination, may not fully grasp what is required. erText: In the 4-mark questions assessed exclusively in terms of AO1, Q1.1 was answered well and good knowledge of the institutions that regulate global systems was in evidence. There was frequent reference to the role of the UN as prompted in the question, but students also showed suitably referred to institutions such as the WTO, IMF and WHO and their roles in global governance. 4-mark questions are point marked. A mark may be awarded where a student makes a single relevant point and subsequent marks awarded (if applicable) where the student develops those points with additional knowledge. To score well in these questions, students should aim to write a clear and focused responses that is are focused directly on the concept being assessed. Knowledge of the key area in the specification is vital and students should aim to construct a direct answer and provide a suitable example. The weaker responses to the 4 mark questions tend to show a poor understanding of the key concept or a vague / unclear awareness of the topic. These responses often confuse ideas and fail to state ideas clearly. For example, in this response the student states that the UN attempts to resolve and prevent conflicts, which is exemplified with reference to the Russia-Ukraine war. Further credit comes from the description of the roles played by both the World Trade Organisation and the World Health Organisation. It scored the maximum 4 marks. The response below was awarded 1 mark as the point about the role of the World Trade Organisation is just about credit-worthy. The rest shows confusion between different organisations and their roles in a global system.

erText: There were also plenty of opportunities in 1.2 and 2.2 for students to demonstrate links within and between the resources. The AO3 (.2) questions provided opportunities for students to demonstrate their geographical skills of analysis and interpretation of a variety of graphical presentations and maps. Level 2 was accessed frequently as students showed an awareness of general patterns and trends, utilising the data for some manipulation and / or identification of anomalies. The resources used in this examination paper included a compound bar graph, scatter graph, maps, dot maps, tables and proportional symbols. There were no calculations or ‘practical tasks’ involved in the AO3 skills this time. In order to gain Level 2 marks, students should draw out the overall patterns or trends of the data, exemplify the points they are making, look for anomalies and try to do more than simply make statements that refer to the basic evidence shown. In many cases it is possible to look at the extremes of the data, provide some basic data manipulation or contrast so that there is evidence of analysis rather than basic description. With the interpretation of the maps, the best answers made use of the map conventions (e.g. scale, direction) and made clear links or contrasts between the two maps. Less successful responses to these questions sometimes fail to identify key trends or patterns, miss clear connections between resources and sometimes not address the question by offering explanation for the data being shown. The example below shows all of these characteristics in that it gives a general overview of both resources, uses some selected data to illustrate this, identifies those countries that do not fit the general pattern and does some data manipulation (difference, percentages). It even provides a little critique of the way the data is presented which is part of the AO3 strand to ‘interpret, analyse and evaluate data and evidence’.

Either, they analyse the resource (doing what they should be doing with the .2 questions), only comment on the resource as a route towards answering the question (so use none of their ‘own knowledge’) or the reverse where they use only their own knowledge (AO1) and do not interface with the resource (AO2). ‘Global governance of the global commons has a direct impact on your life and the

Critically assess the extent to which you agree with this statement.

msText:
‘Global governance of the global commons has a direct impact on
01
4
20
your life and the lives of people across the globe.’
AO1 = 10
AO2 = 10
Critically assess the extent to which you agree with this statement.
AO1 – Knowledge and understanding of the concept of the global
commons and the need to protect them.  Knowledge and understanding
of the geographical consequences of global governance of the global
commons
AO2 – Application of knowledge and understanding to critically assess
the extent to which global governance of the global commons impacts on
the student’s lives and lives of people around the globe.
Notes for answers
The question requires students to make links between different aspects
of the global governance unit.  They need to apply their knowledge of
global governance of the global commons to the impact this governance
might have on their own lives and the lives of others around the globe.
This is a very open question and students can tackle it in a variety of
ways.  Antarctica is likely to be a common example, but there is no
requirement to include it and they do not need to make reference to more
than one global commons.
AO1
• Knowledge and understanding of issues and attempts of global
governance by agencies such as the UN.
• Interactions between the local, regional, national, international and
global scales are fundamental to understanding global governance.
• The concept of the global commons.
• The rights of all to the benefits of the global commons.
Acknowledgement that the rights of all people to sustainable
development must also acknowledge the need to protect the global
commons.
• Threats to Antarctica from tourism and scientific research, fishing and
whaling, the search for minerals.
• Governance of Antarctica and other global commons – international
organisations and NGOs.
• Strategies for enhancing protection of Antarctica and other global
commons.
• Analysis and assessment of the geographical consequences of global
governance for citizens and places in Antarctica and elsewhere to
specifically consider how global governance underlies and impacts on
students’ and other people’s lives across the globe.
AO2
• Analysis of the importance of protecting the global commons in relation
to shared ownership.  The global commons are not owned by a single
nation so global governance is a necessity to ensure they are not
exploited.
• They may consider the concept of the ‘tragedy of the commons’.
Some nations may exploit the commons for their own gain, resulting in
other countries taking more, resulting in unsustainable resource use.
This benefits the citizens of those countries but globally could be
disastrous, for example the depletion of cod stocks in the Atlantic.
• Evaluation of conventions and treaties used to protect the commons.
For example the 1982 UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS)
has not been very successful as many countries refuse to ratify it and
many activities such as bioprospecting are not regulated by it.
• The extent to which global governance is important in achieving
sustainable development for global citizens rather than citizens of
individual nations.  For example, the Paris agreement to reduce
atmospheric carbon is necessary for the planet as a whole, despite
having detrimental impacts on people working in the coal industry.
• Evaluation of the extent to which their global governance has a positive
impact on their own lives.  For example, they may consider their own
well-being knowing there are attempts to reduce carbon emissions into
the atmosphere.
• The extent to which their global governance has a negative impact on
their own lives.  For example, they could consider that the Antarctic
Treaty restricts travel and their own opportunities to view Antarctica.
• Evaluation of the role of international agreements in protecting the
global commons, for example the Paris Agreement to limit carbon
emissions is trying to reduce the impact of climate change on our
oceans and Antarctica.  This could protect people living in coastal
areas at threat from sea-level rise.
• The extent to which there is no direct impact on their lives.  For
example, the international whaling commission banned whaling in the
high seas, however this has no direct impact on them, but indirectly
affects them by preserving whale species and ensuring they will be
around for future generations.
• Alternative futures in terms of different outcomes of global governance
of the global commons would also be relevant.
• Overall conclusion should seek to consider the extent to which they
agree with the statement.  It should be supported by the body of the
text and evidence provided.
Any valid assessment will be credited.

erText: The 20-mark essay questions continue to illustrate the strong subject knowledge, evaluative skills and preparation of many students. These questions differentiate well, and the increasing confidence shown in these was demonstrated with over 60% of entries attaining at least Level 3. The key is always to demonstrably address the question and to ensure that the application of knowledge and understanding (AO2) is evident with AO1 knowledge used in support. The best responses are clearly organised, follow a logical structure and take a clear and sustained line of reasoning before reaching a conclusion based on the evidence provided. At the other end of the scale, less successful responses can be attributed to a number of reasons – maybe the student misreads the question, sometimes they start out with good intent but then drift away from the question focus – a brief plan is often a precursor to a good response. Some students just do not know the relevant subject content – either they did not learn it or failed to effectively revise it. Sometimes responses can include examples that are over-simplified, out-dated or clichéd and there is limited evidence of deep knowledge and understanding. In 1.4 there was strong subject knowledge relating to the governance of the global commons (policies and issues pertaining to Antarctica were most frequently seen) and in 2.4 students demonstrated good knowledge and understating of either their local or distant place study in assessing the role of endogenous factors shaping lived experience. This example of a response to 1.4 shows a very good understanding of the global commons, detailed knowledge and understanding of policies to manage / mitigate impacts on Antarctica and climate change and possible impacts on lives of people around the world. The answer shows a detailed understanding of these approaches and makes effective evaluative statements before coming to a clear conclusion. This was assessed in Level 4 and it was awarded 20 marks. Responses do not need to be ‘perfect’ to be given this mark.

erText: In the 4-mark (AO1) questions, the key point to note was the difficulty some students had with outlining how they used a qualitative data source, such as 2.1, to investigate lived experience in the past in their local place addressing the requirements of the question. A significant proportion simply defined the idea of qualitative data or described a source without linking it to the past lived experience required. 4-mark questions are point marked. A mark may be awarded where a student makes a single relevant point and subsequent marks awarded (if applicable) where the student develops those points with additional knowledge. To score well in these questions, students should aim to write a clear and focused responses that is are focused directly on the concept being assessed. Knowledge of the key area in the specification is vital and students should aim to construct a direct answer and provide a suitable example. The weaker responses to the 4 mark questions tend to show a poor understanding of the key concept or a vague / unclear awareness of the topic. These responses often confuse ideas and fail to state ideas clearly. In the example below, the response has not followed the commands of the question and whilst they it describes the role of a qualitative source and give a number of examples it does not say how it was used to investigate past lived experience in their local place. This response received no credit.

erText: There were also plenty of opportunities in 1.2 and 2.2 for students to demonstrate links within and between the resources. The AO3 (.2) questions provided opportunities for students to demonstrate their geographical skills of analysis and interpretation of a variety of graphical presentations and maps. Level 2 was accessed frequently as students showed an awareness of general patterns and trends, utilising the data for some manipulation and / or identification of anomalies. The resources used in this examination paper included a compound bar graph, scatter graph, maps, dot maps, tables and proportional symbols. There were no calculations or ‘practical tasks’ involved in the AO3 skills this time. In order to gain Level 2 marks, students should draw out the overall patterns or trends of the data, exemplify the points they are making, look for anomalies and try to do more than simply make statements that refer to the basic evidence shown. In many cases it is possible to look at the extremes of the data, provide some basic data manipulation or contrast so that there is evidence of analysis rather than basic description. With the interpretation of the maps, the best answers made use of the map conventions (e.g. scale, direction) and made clear links or contrasts between the two maps. Less successful responses to these questions sometimes fail to identify key trends or patterns, miss clear connections between resources and sometimes not address the question by offering explanation for the data being shown. In this example the student follows the same approach with the maps from Q2.2. The overall pattern is noted, there are links between the two resources, data is used in support and anomalies are identifies. This also obtained the full 6 marks.

As an example in 2.4 a student ,referenced the redevelopment of the Albert Docks in Liverpool as a cause of deindustrialisation rather than understanding the complete timeline.

erText: The AO3 (.2) questions provided opportunities for students to demonstrate their geographical skills of analysis and interpretation of a variety of graphical presentations and maps. Level 2 was accessed frequently as students showed an awareness of general patterns and trends, utilising the data for some manipulation and / or identification of anomalies. The resources used in this examination paper included a compound bar graph, scatter graph, maps, dot maps, tables and proportional symbols. There were no calculations or ‘practical tasks’ involved in the AO3 skills this time. In order to gain Level 2 marks, students should draw out the overall patterns or trends of the data, exemplify the points they are making, look for anomalies and try to do more than simply make statements that refer to the basic evidence shown. In many cases it is possible to look at the extremes of the data, provide some basic data manipulation or contrast so that there is evidence of analysis rather than basic description. With the interpretation of the maps, the best answers made use of the map conventions (e.g. scale, direction) and made clear links or contrasts between the two maps. Less successful responses to these questions sometimes fail to identify key trends or patterns, miss clear connections between resources and sometimes not address the question by offering explanation for the data being shown.

erText: The 6- and 9-mark questions in each section referring to stimulus material (.3) were attempted with some confidence. Students used their own knowledge and understanding alongside the resources to answer the question and this was most effectively done in the options (3.3, 4.3 and 5.3). Each scenario required students to consider an area of the specification (mitigation strategies for non-communicable diseases, edge cities and the environmental impacts of dams / barrages), link the resource and utilise their own knowledge. Students are clearly well prepared for these questions and relatively few gave descriptive or analytical responses based solely on the novel resource. The AO1/AO2 questions using a novel resource, aim to test students’ abilities to apply their knowledge of a key idea to the situation presented and bring in some of their own knowledge to support their argument. In these questions, AO2 is more heavily weighted than AO1 and therefore the argument along with the application from the resource is key but ‘own knowledge’ as well also gains credit. When students do not score so well on these questions it can usually be put down to one of three things. Either, they analyse the resource (doing what they should be doing with the .2 questions), only comment on the resource as a route towards answering the question (so use none of their ‘own knowledge’) or the reverse where they use only their own knowledge (AO1) and do not interface with the resource (AO2). Relatively few students gave solely descriptive accounts of the novel resources provided in the .3 questions. Where this did occur, students only obtained credit in Level 1. In the next example, the student engaged with the resource and quoted evidence from it to present their view that Le Defense is an edge city but shows little actual knowledge of the edge city concept. It was assessed at the top of Level 1 and awarded 3.

erText: The 9-mark questions in the options all showed a mean score well into Level 2 with some good knowledge and evaluation of sustainable urban drainage, managing soil problems and the relationship between physical and energy mix. There was good subject specific knowledge evident in the .4 9-mark questions in the options, but students would be advised to include relevant examples of places / situations to add weight to their theoretical knowledge and assessment. These questions assess students’ subject knowledge and application within the specification units. Responses should have a balance of AO1 knowledge and AO2 evaluation / assessment in which the subject knowledge is applied to actually answer the question. Good answers show detailed knowledge and a clear and explicit evaluation / assessment. Less successful responses either did not understand the key concept being tested, so students who did not know about sustainable urban drainage systems, the management of soil problems or the links between energy mix and physical geography would clearly not score well. A lack of depth of knowledge or a failure to fully assess / evaluate the issue would also lead to lower marks. In the example below (from 3.3 Contemporary urban environments) the response shows some basic knowledge of SUDs (they refer to permeable pavements and swales), but limited understanding of how they work and there is little evaluation of their use as ways of managing water movement through urban catchments. It was given some credit at the top of Level 1, 3 marks.

erText: The 20-mark essay questions continue to illustrate the strong subject knowledge, evaluative skills and preparation of many students. These questions differentiate well, and the increasing confidence shown in these was demonstrated with over 60% of entries attaining at least Level 3. The key is always to demonstrably address the question and to ensure that the application of knowledge and understanding (AO2) is evident with AO1 knowledge used in support. The best responses are clearly organised, follow a logical structure and take a clear and sustained line of reasoning before reaching a conclusion based on the evidence provided. At the other end of the scale, less successful responses can be attributed to a number of reasons – maybe the student misreads the question, sometimes they start out with good intent but then drift away from the question focus – a brief plan is often a precursor to a good response. Some students just do not know the relevant subject content – either they did not learn it or failed to effectively revise it. Sometimes responses can include examples that are over-simplified, out-dated or clichéd and there is limited evidence of deep knowledge and understanding. Q3.5 also highlighted a lack of knowledge regarding urban regeneration policies from 1979. Whilst the specification does not list any particular policies, a number of responses only referred to contemporary (post 2012) urban strategies. In the response to 3.5 below, the student doesn’t really get to grips with the question and does not engage with the approaches to urban regeneration since 1979 perhaps this was not learned or revised well?. However they do attempt to discuss aspects of environmental sustainability within urban areas and there is some evaluation as well as reaching a conclusion. The response is partial, assessed as Level 2, 7 marks.

Outline the concept of the ‘ecological footprint’.

Point marked

Notes for answers
• Ecological footprint is the area of land needed to provide the
necessary resources and absorb the waste generated by a community
(1).
• The concept of the ecological footprint can be considered at different
scales (1) such as individuals / households / communities / countries
(1) (d)
• It includes factors such as the amount of food consumed (1) the waste
that is produced (1), the carbon emissions produced from human
activities eg transport (1), energy consumed through daily tasks (1).
There are many activities that contribute to the ecological footprint so
credit valid points.
• The ecological footprint can be reduced by managing / adjusting
human activities – these ideas can be credited as part of the concept.
• Ecological footprints measure the impact that individuals and societies
have on the Earth’s resources (1).  Ecological footprints are generally
higher in HICs where resource use and waste production are high (1).
• Ecological footprints determine whether the planet is large enough to
cope with the number of people living on it (1).  It can be expressed as
the number of planets needed to sustain a population of a country (1)
(d).
• The ‘Earth overshoot’ day is related to ecological footprint.  This is the
date each year when the global demand for resources exceeds the
capacity for earth to regenerate those resources (1).  In 2021 the date
was July 29th, in 2022 it was July 28th and in 2023 it was August 2nd,
so just over halfway through the year, Earth is in ecological deficit (1)
(d).
• Ecological footprints consider the balance between assets and
demands on resources (1).  Biocapacity represents the assets and
shows the earth’s productive land areas such as pasture, forests and
fisheries (1) (d).  These areas can also act as sinks for waste and
emissions (1) (d).

erText: The 6- and 9-mark questions in each section referring to stimulus material (.3) were attempted with some confidence. Students used their own knowledge and understanding alongside the resources to answer the question and this was most effectively done in the options (3.3, 4.3 and 5.3). Each scenario required students to consider an area of the specification (mitigation strategies for non-communicable diseases, edge cities and the environmental impacts of dams / barrages), link the resource and utilise their own knowledge. Students are clearly well prepared for these questions and relatively few gave descriptive or analytical responses based solely on the novel resource. The AO1/AO2 questions using a novel resource, aim to test students’ abilities to apply their knowledge of a key idea to the situation presented and bring in some of their own knowledge to support their argument. In these questions, AO2 is more heavily weighted than AO1 and therefore the argument along with the application from the resource is key but ‘own knowledge’ as well also gains credit. When students do not score so well on these questions it can usually be put down to one of three things. Either, they analyse the resource (doing what they should be doing with the .2 questions), only comment on the resource as a route towards answering the question (so use none of their ‘own knowledge’) or the reverse where they use only their own knowledge (AO1) and do not interface with the resource (AO2). Relatively few students gave solely descriptive accounts of the novel resources provided in the .3 questions. Where this did occur, students only obtained credit in Level 1.

erText: The 9-mark questions in the options all showed a mean score well into Level 2 with some good knowledge and evaluation of sustainable urban drainage, managing soil problems and the relationship between physical and energy mix. There was good subject specific knowledge evident in the .4 9-mark questions in the options, but students would be advised to include relevant examples of places / situations to add weight to their theoretical knowledge and assessment. These questions assess students’ subject knowledge and application within the specification units. Responses should have a balance of AO1 knowledge and AO2 evaluation / assessment in which the subject knowledge is applied to actually answer the question. A lack of depth of knowledge or a failure to fully assess / evaluate the issue would also lead to lower marks.

erText: The 20-mark essay questions continue to illustrate the strong subject knowledge, evaluative skills and preparation of many students. These questions differentiate well, and the increasing confidence shown in these was demonstrated with over 60% of entries attaining at least Level 3. The key is always to demonstrably address the question and to ensure that the application of knowledge and understanding (AO2) is evident with AO1 knowledge used in support. The best responses are clearly organised, follow a logical structure and take a clear and sustained line of reasoning before reaching a conclusion based on the evidence provided. At the other end of the scale, less successful responses can be attributed to a number of reasons – maybe the student misreads the question, sometimes they start out with good intent but then drift away from the question focus – a brief plan is often a precursor to a good response. Some students just do not know the relevant subject content – either they did not learn it or failed to effectively revise it. Sometimes responses can include examples that are over-simplified, out-dated or clichéd and there is limited evidence of deep knowledge and understanding. The response below is from 4.5. It uses Japan as the example of a country experiencing demographic transition and shows some valid AO1 knowledge, but there are some very simplistic views of the environment (hilly, so people are fitter and there are lots of trees so lots of oxygen). It does attempt to answer the question and reaches a conclusion but overall the response is partial and was assessed as a Level 2 response and given 7 marks.

erText: The 9-mark questions in the options all showed a mean score well into Level 2 with some good knowledge and evaluation of sustainable urban drainage, managing soil problems and the relationship between physical and energy mix. There was good subject specific knowledge evident in the .4 9-mark questions in the options, but students would be advised to include relevant examples of places / situations to add weight to their theoretical knowledge and assessment. These questions assess students’ subject knowledge and application within the specification units. Responses should have a balance of AO1 knowledge and AO2 evaluation / assessment in which the subject knowledge is applied to actually answer the question. Good answers show detailed knowledge and a clear and explicit evaluation / assessment. Less successful responses either did not understand the key concept being tested, so students who did not know about sustainable urban drainage systems, the management of soil problems or the links between energy mix and physical geography would clearly not score well. A lack of depth of knowledge or a failure to fully assess / evaluate the issue would also lead to lower marks. In this example drawn from the Resource security option, the student uses Iceland and France as their contrasting areas of study and makes an immediate statement regarding the extent of the link between physical geography and energy mix in Iceland. The response shows good AO1 knowledge and synoptic links to the physical geography specification. There is detailed knowledge of the background to the energy mix of both Iceland and France and the contrasts are clear. This was assessed as Level 3 and awarded 8 marks.

erText: The 20-mark essay questions continue to illustrate the strong subject knowledge, evaluative skills and preparation of many students. These questions differentiate well, and the increasing confidence shown in these was demonstrated with over 60% of entries attaining at least Level 3. The key is always to demonstrably address the question and to ensure that the application of knowledge and understanding (AO2) is evident with AO1 knowledge used in support. The best responses are clearly organised, follow a logical structure and take a clear and sustained line of reasoning before reaching a conclusion based on the evidence provided. At the other end of the scale, less successful responses can be attributed to a number of reasons – maybe the student misreads the question, sometimes they start out with good intent but then drift away from the question focus – a brief plan is often a precursor to a good response. Some students just do not know the relevant subject content – either they did not learn it or failed to effectively revise it. Sometimes responses can include examples that are over-simplified, out-dated or clichéd and there is limited evidence of deep knowledge and understanding. A further example of a Level 4 response is taken from the Resource security option, 5.5 below. It shows detailed knowledge and understanding of the topic, utilises examples well and brings in some concepts showing wider geographical understanding. It also ends with a clear evaluative conclusion. This was awarded 18 marks in Level 4.

erText: These skills were tested whenever a stimulus resource was used, or numerical data needed to be engaged with. On this paper this was the 6-mark skills question on each option, i.e. 1.4, 2.4, 3.4, 4.4 and 5.4. The main issue here was that many students demonstrated AO2 type answers by applying their knowledge, offering reasons for patterns for example, or too simply lifting data directly from the resource. This was not the question. The command ‘analyse’ in this context, simply required students to interface with the data, manipulate, and deconstruct the information. Where two resources were provided, for example two maps or two graphs, it is logical, and expected, that responses will seek to identify any links or connections between the information provided. This question differentiated well, with a mean mark of 3.85/6. Despite 63% of students scoring in Level 2 only around one third achieved 5 or 6 marks suggesting that many found this question challenging. Many responses failed to go beyond lifting numbers from the figures or very simple description. Responses like this struggled to reach the top of Level 1. It was envisaged that having two relatively straightforward graphs would allow students to make straightforward comparisons and make use of the data, which few did. The best answers supported their points with clear use and manipulation of data, whilst weaker responses simply lifted values from the figures. Other high-quality answers made explicit attempts to make links between the two figures and give comparisons of the different amounts of carbon stored and the area of the biomes. Although, less of an issue than in some previous series, some responses did quickly drift into explanation of possible reasons for the differences in the size of the carbon stores. This is AO2 and was not valid in this AO3 question.

erText: This question combined both AO1 and AO2 elements. This required students to make links within the Water and Carbon Cycles specification, with specific reference to human activity and the hydrosphere as a store of carbon. The average mark for this question was 3.9 suggesting that most students found this to be a challenging question. Most were able to identify human activities that affected the carbon cycle in general, the burning of fossil fuels for example, but few seemed familiar with the hydrosphere as a store of carbon. It was envisaged that accessing Level 2 would be quite straightforward. Responses were required to identify that the burning of fossil fuels and the associated release of CO2 into the atmosphere was leading to climate change, increasing in atmospheric temperatures and causing the oceans to warm. More CO2 in the atmosphere is leading to more CO2 dissolving into the sea, therefore increasing the size of the hydrospheric store of carbon. However, these warmer waters are then less able to absorb/take CO2 from the atmosphere. Warming may ultimately lead to the oceans becoming a net carbon source rather than carbon sink. The level of specific detail given in support would then determine how far the response could move through the mark scheme to the higher levels. The 18% of responses that did reach Level 3 often exhibited excellent knowledge and understanding of the various chemical processes at work as human activities impacted the carbon cycle. Some also assessed how attempts at mitigating climate change could also impact the hydrosphere, for example utilising the deep oceans to sequester excess carbon.

erText: This question proved very accessible and around 75% of students provided clear and /or detailed responses achieving in Level 3 or higher. These generally scored well with respect to AO1, with clear and detailed knowledge of specific human activities happening in a specific named tropical rainforest. Clearly some responses failed to go beyond making sweeping statements about whole continental scale forests, for example “deforestation in the Amazon leads to increased runoff.” However, some gave very clear details about specific locations within a named rainforest and were able to quantify the impacts of the human activity, for example naming specific dams and the impact they had had on the discharge of a river, or changes in specific rates of evapotranspiration. There were many interesting case studies used to support answers and most did focus on the Amazon. Some students struggled as they had little focus on specific aspects of the water cycle, with limited knowledge and understanding shown of specific inputs, flows, stores, and outputs.

erText: This question performed well but proved challenging for some students. 34% achieved full marks, whilst 16% scored zero and the mean was 1.79/3. The best responses clearly understood the process of longshore/littoral drift and offered a succinct sequential answer. These responses generally started with the idea that waves approach the coast from the same direction as the prevailing wind. With the swash picking up material and moving it up the beach in the same direction and backwash returning sediment perpendicularly back down the beach due to gravity. erText: These skills were tested whenever a stimulus resource was used, or numerical data needed to be engaged with. On this paper this was the 6-mark skills question on each option, i.e. 1.4, 2.4, 3.4, 4.4 and 5.4. The main issue here was that many students demonstrated AO2 type answers by applying their knowledge, offering reasons for patterns for example, or too simply lifting data directly from the resource. This was not the question. The command ‘analyse’ in this context, simply required students to interface with the data, manipulate, and deconstruct the information. Where two resources were provided, for example two maps or two graphs, it is logical, and expected, that responses will seek to identify any links or connections between the information provided. Like the other AO3 skills questions on the paper, this proved challenging for some students. The mean mark was 3.48/6. Less than 16% of responses achieved 5 or 6 marks. Very few went beyond making very basic descriptive statements with data lifted from the figure. Responses like this struggled to reach the top of Level 1. It was envisaged that students would be able to clearly see that in some parts of Europe, sea levels had risen relative to the land and in others it had fallen. This would have allowed for clear comparisons to be made. The extent to which a response could then move through the higher level would be determined by the level of map detail and manipulation of data used in support. The weakest responses did not show that they understood that the map showed the rise and fall of sea levels. Others showed little understanding of the data, making statements like “much of Finland had -4.0 fall in sea level”. Other responses did not score well as they quickly drifted into explanation or possible reasons for proportions of people at risk in different scenarios. This constituted AO2 and therefore was not valid in this AO3 question. The best responses had evidence of detailed use of map skills and clear handling of the numerical data.

• Distinctively coastal processes: marine: erosion – hydraulic action, wave

AO2
• Responses are likely to be heavily influenced by the exemplification

• Assessment may focus on the direct impact that mass movement

have on shaping cliff profile features. For example, in April 2021 a 300
m long stretch of coast close to Weymouth in Dorset slumped and an
estimated 4 000 tonnes of material collapsed and was deposited lower
down the cliff and completely covered the beach below. This rotational
slumping completely altered the profile of 300 m of cliffs and completely
covered a significant area of beach.

processes may have in contributing to other processes that
subsequently shape coastal landforms. For example, by adding material

picked up and transported to be deposited elsewhere.

erText: This question combined both AO1 and AO2 elements. This required students to make links within the Coastal Systems and Landscapes specification, with specific reference to mass movement and coastal landforms. The average mark for this question was only 4.07/9 and only 17% achieved marks in the Level 3 range. This suggests that many found this question to be very challenging. For many the issue seemed to be a lack of familiarity with the concept of mass movement. Many confused this with processes of erosion, weathering, or transportation and so often struggled to move out of Level 1. Better responses often had clear understanding of processes, such as rotational slumping and had accurate descriptions. However, these often did not then make a link to the shaping of landforms. Answers such as this generally got stuck in Level 2. The best responses gave clear and detailed understanding of more than one mass movement process and made explicit links to how the process affected the shape of specific landforms. Some responses sought to assess the role of mass movement compared to other processes. This was credit worthy, although to score well, there still needed to be knowledge and understanding of mass movement as that was the specification area that the question was targeting. Although not explicitly asked for in the question, many good responses had illustration from specific local-scale coastal examples. This often enhanced the quality of the answer.

erText: With a mean mark of 5.43 out of 9 and almost 1/3 of students reaching Level 3, this question provided accessible to many. Most were able to identify meltwater as having the capacity to erode, transport and deposit material, hence creating new landforms. Many responses focused on eskers, kames, and the outwash plain, showing clear knowledge and understanding of the specification content. The very best responses engaged with how the role of meltwater in their formation made these landforms distinctive. For example, being composed of smoothed and rounded material, or having evidence of sorting of material. A relatively small number of responses confused fluvioglacial landforms with periglacial landforms and therefore did not score well.

AO1

• The global distribution of past and present cold environments (polar,
alpine, glacial and periglacial) and of areas affected by the Pleistocene
glaciations.

AO2
• It is likely that the direction taken will depend upon the types of cold
environments chosen as exemplification.
• Assessment may focus on a range of timescales: o Assessment of
the extent to which the distribution of cold environments changed
during the Pleistocene glaciations, over the glacial and interglacial
cycles between about 1.6 million and 12 000 YBP. Responses may
come to the view that over this timescale there was very extensive
change in the distribution of cold environments, but that it occurred
over geological timescales. Examples may be given in support.
o Assessment of the extent to which the distribution of cold
environments has changed during the Holocene, over the last
12 000 years. Here, responses may give more specific details in
support of the distribution of specific polar, alpine, glacial and
periglacial environments. o The above may lead into an
assessment of the current distribution and extent of the different
cold environments. Responses may provide assessment of the

different cold environments.

distribution of cold environments will be speculative.

assessment of the rate of possible future climate change and the impact

in polar environments will accelerate, reducing the magnitude of the

erText: This question differentiated well, but many found it quite challenging. 63% of students were able to produce good answers and reached Level 3 or higher. The mean mark was only 10.8 out of 20, suggesting that only a small proportion were able to provide the clarity or detail required to reach the very highest levels of the mark scheme. The best answers fully understood the question and gave plenty of detail about the extent of cold environments in the past, mostly focusing on the time since the last glacial maximum about 20,000 years before present. These responses often gave the view that, at this time, cold environments had covered very considerable areas of the Earth, and that this area has been decreasing ever since. For those that fully targeted the question, they then gave an account of how the extent of most cold environments is likely to decrease in the future due to current and future climate change. Only the very best suggested that the extent of periglacial environments may in fact extend before decreasing. As is quite often the case on the Cold Environments 20-mark question, a significant number of students wanted to give a rehearsed human geography answer to this physical geography question. For example, many talked about negative economic and social impacts of global warming on Swiss ski resorts. Unless answers like this explicitly referred to aspects such as shrinking glaciers or rising snow lines it was difficult for these to gain much credit even in Level 2. Likewise, responses that took Alaska as their inspiration, often gave a rehearsed response about the challenges this environment poses to people living there, and without reference to the changing sizes of glaciers or areas of permafrost etc, these too struggled to gain credit.

erText: These skills were tested whenever a stimulus resource was used, or numerical data needed to be engaged with. On this paper this was the 6-mark skills question on each option, i.e. 1.4, 2.4, 3.4, 4.4 and 5.4. The main issue here was that many students demonstrated AO2 type answers by applying their knowledge, offering reasons for patterns for example, or too simply lifting data directly from the resource. This was not the question. The command ‘analyse’ in this context, simply required students to interface with the data, manipulate, and deconstruct the information. Where two resources were provided, for example two maps or two graphs, it is logical, and expected, that responses will seek to identify any links or connections between the information provided. As in other series and on other parts of this paper, this AO3 skills question proved quite challenging for many. The mean mark was 3.23, but only 13% scored 5 or 6 marks. Those scoring well, confidently used and manipulated evidence from the maps. It was envisaged that having two relatively straightforward maps would allow students to make straightforward comparisons and make use of the data, which few did. Some weaker responses appeared to struggle with the concept of population density and so responses became confusing or unclear as they suggested, for instance, that 6,000 people lived in Bangkok. Inevitably, other responses that did not score well, again appeared unprepared for these AO3 skills questions, and sought to explain or give reasons for the data, which would be AO2 content and so therefore not credit worthy.

Notes for answers AO1
• Impact and human responses as evidenced by a recent wildfire event.
• Nature, forms and potential impacts of natural hazards.
• Nature of wildfires. Impacts: primary/secondary, environmental, social,
economic, political. Short- and long-term responses; risk management
designed to reduce the impacts of the hazard through preparedness,
mitigation, prevention and adaptation.
• The concept of place and the importance of place in human life and
experience.
• Factors contributing to the character of places:
o Endogenous: location, topography, physical geography, land use,
built environment and infrastructure, demographic and economic
characteristics.
o Exogenous: relationships with other places.
AO2
• Responses are expected to show an understanding of the nature of the
impacts of a recent wildfire event. There should be clear recognition of
the learning from the Changing Places unit in evaluating how the
characteristics of the place were affected by the wildfire event.
Reciting learned case study material does not constitute AO2. It is the
integration of the place study ideas and concepts which allow access to
AO2.
• There are any number of recent wildfire events to which candidates can
refer, therefore their overall evaluation of how the characteristics of
place were affected by the event will depend on the case study provided.
• When evaluating the impacts of the recent wildfire event, candidates
may address a range of impacts including: primary, secondary,
environmental, social, economic, political.
• The above are legitimate elements to include in a response, but
evaluation must focus on how the characteristics of the place were
affected by the wildfire event.

depend on the recent wildfire event. Responses are likely to consider a
range of characteristics and are free to choose the ones they wish to
focus on. The place characteristics will depend on the chosen location
and any logical and relevant characteristics of the case study location
could be valid.
• The key is that there is clear evaluation and judgement of how the
characteristics of place were affected by a recent wildfire event.
• In 2016 Fort McMurray, Alberta, Canada, experienced a very significant
wildfire that had widespread impacts. Five years after the event it was
reported that the visual character and character of the built environment
had changed significantly as a result of the fire. Many of these changes
related to lessons learnt from the impacts of the 2016 fire. Timber
framed homes had been replaced with stone and concrete houses with
more open space between them. Where forests and vegetation had
been allowed to grow close to and around built-up areas prior to the
fire, the vegetation had either not been replanted or had been removed.
One housing area that had to be completely rebuilt following the fire,
was subsequently laid out along a wide, straight central road, rather
than its original curvilinear street pattern, so as to speed up any future
evacuation should a wildfire hit the town again.

that the impacts of the fire led to very significant impacts on the
character of the town in terms of its visual look, built environment and
pattern of land use.
Credit any valid evaluation as long as the argument is coherent and
feasible.
erText: This question proved to quite challenging for many and had a mean score of only 4.35.Only 13% is responses achieved Level 3. Only the very best responses had clear and detailed knowledge and understanding of an appropriate wildfire event, whilst identifying that this was across specification question, requiring application of knowledge and understanding from the Changing Places unit. Where the link was identified the best responses identified specific economic, social, demographic, or environmental characteristics of place that had been impacted by the wildfire event. Many responses often did not focus on the impacts at the scale of the local place, i.e. referring to the “Black Saturday Bushfires in Australia,” and whilst most did identify impacts, it was hard to see any link to specific characteristics of place. There were some excellent responses that focused on specific impacts of fires in Fort McMurray or more recently in California, where individual neighbourhoods or areas were given as exemplar material. Other responses sought to compare different wildfires. These often did not score well as depth was often lost with this approach. As with Q4.5 above, many students made comparisons between 2 case studies, which could be creditworthy, however, the specification is clear that only one case study is required.

erText: These skills were tested whenever a stimulus resource was used, or numerical data needed to be engaged with. On this paper this was the 6-mark skills question on each option, i.e. 1.4, 2.4, 3.4, 4.4 and 5.4. The main issue here was that many students demonstrated AO2 type answers by applying their knowledge, offering reasons for patterns for example, or too simply lifting data directly from the resource. This was not the question. The command ‘analyse’ in this context, simply required students to interface with the data, manipulate, and deconstruct the information. Where two resources were provided, for example two maps or two graphs, it is logical, and expected, that responses will seek to identify any links or connections between the information provided. As in other series and on other parts of this paper, this AO3 skills question proved to be quite challenging for many. The mean mark was 3.57, but only 20% score 5 or 6. Those scoring well, confidently used and manipulated evidence from the maps. It was envisaged that having two relatively straightforward maps would allow students to make straightforward comparisons and make use of the data, which few did. The link or connection between the two maps was quite obvious, and encouraged responses to be comparative. However, many responses struggled to go beyond lifting and basic description. Some responses did not engage with the key on Figure 5a. The best responses confidently talked about areas that were warmer and cooler than the mean. Whilst others were quite poorly expressed, and were confused for example, describing central Staten Island as having a temperature of minus 4. Other responses that did not score well appeared unprepared for these AO3 skills questions, and sought to explain or give reasons for the data, which would be AO2 content and so therefore not credit worthy.

erText: This question differentiated well and many provided good quality answers. The mean mark was 5.47 out of 9 and 30% scored in Level 3. The best responses had clear knowledge and understanding of specific environmental problems in a named urban area, whilst identifying that this was the cross specification question requiring application of knowledge and understanding from the Changing Places unit. Where the link was identified, the best responses had very specific environment problems, e.g. air pollution, poor waste management or even excessive summer heat, and were able to make clear links to specific impacts on aspects of peoples’ lives. Answers that did not score well were often quite generic or lacked any clear attempt to link the environmental problems to the lives of people and their experience of the named urban area. A very significant number of responses tried to compare 1 urban area to another. This could score credit. However, this approach made it difficult for students to develop the specific detail required for the higher level. Focusing on just one urban area, would have allowed scope for more specific detail to be developed.

erText: Like other 20-mark questions this differentiated quite well, with a mean of 12.23 and over 70% reached Level 3 or higher. The best answers showed clear and/or detailed knowledge and understanding of the urban water cycle, and explicitly referred to specific inputs, flows, stores, and outputs in the cycle. Many of these responses noted how urban areas influence precipitation, infiltration rates and then levels of overland flow. Others linked aspects of the urban heat island effect to rates of evaporation and then possible links to thunderstorms. There were some responses that looked at the impact of urban areas on different stores of water, for example the impact of abstraction on ground water. These could all score well, as long as there was also clear and detailed assessment. Although, the question did not require a case study, many of the best responses did support their points with reference to named locations. This often added to the quality of the AO1 element of the answer. Some appeared to try to give a rehearsed response about specific examples of SUDs or river restoration.This was credit worthy as long as there was a clear attempt to target aspects of the water cycle.

erText: This question was generally unsuccessful in terms of the quality of responses. This was an AO1 knowledge question, taken from the section on quantitative and qualitative skills. Just over a quarter of students did not access any marks. However, it did differentiate well and nearly a third of students gained at least 2 out of 3 marks. The mark scheme was broadened to allow credit for a generic advantage of quantitative data. Credit was also given for a general overview of what quantitative data can measure in terms of change, for example changes in housing types. The higher-level responses tended to be those that were able to link a source of quantitative data to the context of an actual example of how it showed change over time, for example considering the usefulness of census data in showing how occupations had changed. erText: Overall, students coped reasonably well with the questions in Section A, performing especially well on questions 1.1, 1.2, 1.4 and Q1.6, the 20-mark essay. This question proved slightly more accessible than 1.4 in 2024. Over 50% of students accessed Level 2 on this paper, but half of these were at the lower end of L2. Fewer than 5% got all 6 marks. Most students attempted to seek connection between the two maps noting the variations in London for example compared to the northwest of England. Most students were also able to consider spatial patterns shown in Figure 1a. The more successful answers look at an overview of the patterns in 1a and then drilled down to consider the variations in the spatial pattern in Figure 1b, for example noting that the east of England had the highest change in 1a, but this was not clearly demonstrated in 1b with only one area showing the highest population change. Many used accurate data manipulation in support. Lowerachieving students were still too reliant on straight lift of data, alongside a pedestrian description of population change in each region, often gaining little credit. These students often neglected to use any data in support, simply stating that Wales had the lowest population change for example. Some students also used data inaccurately, for example not understanding that each colour represented a band of change, stating that one area in the southeast of England had a 23% increase. On a positive note, drift into explanation was minimal and the compound nature of the graphs was clearly understood by most students.

gender, socio-economic status, ethnicity and other factors.
• Place attachment can be affected by how a place is represented.  For
example, community groups in a local place may actively encourage a
feeling of ‘belonging’ or local councils may present a place positively.
• Place attachment may be influenced by media such as advertising
campaigns or social media, such as local online community forums.
• Place attachment may be influenced by continuity and change in a
local place and how this is perceived by the people who live there.
• A conclusion should make a judgement about the importance of factors
which have influenced place attachment in this place.
Credit any other valid assessment.
erText: A small number of students chose the same place for the local place in question 1.5 and a distant place in question 1.6. These were both credited. Generally, students did not perform as well on this question as question 1.6. However, performance was much stronger than question 1.5 in 2024. More than double the number of students achieved L3 compared to 2024. The stem statement seemed to be clearly understood by most students. The stem was meant to prompt discussion about the importance of factors affecting attachment to place. Although this approach was adopted by some students, they were in the minority. Instead, many attempted a more theoretical approach in their responses, focusing largely on demonstrating their understanding of the meaning of place attachment. They tended to focus on the psycho-geographical elements such as memories, sense of belonging or identity, media perception, emotional attachment, positive or negative feelings, etc. There was far less emphasis on the assessment of factors that make people feel attached to places. Many students did not focus on their choice of place but gave generic reasons for place attachment, which whilst creditworthy, did not aid clarity of argument. Nonetheless, many clear theoretical arguments and discussions were presented in the context of the local place and over 80% of students achieved Level 2 credit. The more successful responses were clearly those using their local place examples to support their arguments suggesting two or more factors that affected place attachment and then using a strong conclusion to weigh up the importance of the factors.

erText: Overall, students coped reasonably well with the questions in Section A, performing especially well on questions 1.1, 1.2, 1.4 and Q1.6, the 20-mark essay. However, a recurring finding was the over-reliance on place-based knowledge rather than using it to support the arguments made in response to the question. This was particularly evident in question 1.6. A small number of students chose the same place for the local place in question 1.5 and a distant place in question 1.6. These were both credited. This question was, well handled by most students, with a slightly stronger performance than that in 2024. 66% attained at least Level 3 credit and over 12% reached Level 4 outcomes. Less than 5% achieved Level 1. The question gave the opportunity for many students to adapt their knowledge and understanding of the impact of economic or demographic change on the present-day characteristics of a distant place they had studied. In that sense it was a relatively ‘open’ and more typical ‘changing places’ question that linked processes triggering change in a place, to the various outcomes in terms of place characteristics. Students generally used their place knowledge well and supplied narratives that clearly identified a range of relevant economic and demographic processes such as deindustrialisation, migration, globalisation, regeneration and others. Many interesting narratives about past and present processes of development were presented and, in most cases, these were applied well to the distant place studied. Sometimes there was more emphasis on a historical narrative, with a lack of consideration of present-day characteristics. The process of economic and / or demographic change was usually covered well. However, it was the extent to which these determined present-day characteristics of a place that often lacked some development, support or clarity in many answers. For this question, as suggested in the synopsis above, the assessment element (AO2) of responses and application of knowledge and understanding to the question was often implicit throughout the essay, rather than more clearly expressed. The implicit nature of some responses was nonetheless still effective and creditworthy in stronger, more sophisticated responses which integrated their application (AO2) alongside their AO1 content and provided substantial development, elaboration or support. However, in lower-level responses, the application element did not always come across as clearly and some students relied heavily on only basic evaluative statements in their introduction and in brief, limited conclusions to gain their AO2 credit for this question. Students were required to choose either economic or demographic change, however many chose to cover both. Sometimes they used one as a counterargument, a perfectly creditable response to the question. However, some considered both as separate accounts. Credit was given where the change could be considered as both economic and demographic. These accounts tended to lack a sustained line of reasoning and were unable to achieve the higher marks. It should also be noted that, as on last year’s paper, a noticeable minority of students used more than one ‘distant place’ in their response, which went against the rubric of the question. In these cases, as usual, the whole response was considered but only one place (that was better used to address the question) and any general points were credited. Students should be made aware of this when seeing questions that clearly ask for only one place to be included in their answer.

erText: This question is a good example of why it is important to ensure that all the geographical skills in 3.4 of the specification are covered. Many students simply did not know what coding was or understand how it might be used in a field study. Nearly one fifth of all students did not even attempt this question and only around 15% scored two marks. Over a third of students attempting the question were unable to achieve credit. Those who did access marks were able to describe how you might highlight words and classify or group them. Some students went on to suggest how this might be used, considering frequency analysis or use of word – clouds.

erText: This question also proved challenging for students. They needed to suggest sources of background reading and suggest how these would be useful. Over 40% of students were unable to access marks as they did not identify a source, simply stating for example ‘it would be useful to know the number of tourists’, or they just stated the source without stating its usefulness for example ‘a newspaper’. Students should be encouraged to make sure they address all parts of the question. The most successful answers were where they were able to draw on their own fieldwork experience and suggest good sources of background reading, for example ‘Census data would allow us to see the occupations of the local population’.

erText: Most students were able to access this question, with over 80% of students scoring at least one mark. Again, this question illustrates the importance of reading the question carefully as some students neglected to realise that this was sampling in relation to questionnaires and wrote about sampling pebbles for example. A few students didn’t understand the concept of sampling and wrote about the method of constructing a questionnaire instead, therefore they were unable to score marks. The most successful answers included more than one sampling technique with clear justification of why it was an appropriate technique, drawing on their own experiences for inspiration. It was possible to gain full marks using only one technique but most students choosing only one, did not develop their answers fully enough to secure more than one or two marks. Students should also be discouraged from writing ‘it was quick and easy’ without any further elaboration. In such questions, it must be clear why the technique was quick and easy and why that was relevant to the fieldwork data collection.

erText: In general, there appeared to be an improved understanding of the structure of their own fieldwork among students, compared to relatively recent years. Most students were able to articulate a clear aim that was rooted in a specific location. In recent series there has been a more obvious grasp of the different elements that make up a geographical investigation and how they are linked. However, in 2025 they performed less successfully than in 2024, particularly on question 2.5, where they were less secure on the planning of fieldwork and how this linked to outcomes. Questions concerning geographical ideas / theory often seem to be more challenging for students, as they often think they need to provide an elaborate theory or model to link this to, rather than just reflecting on their expectations and aims. In this question they simply needed to consider the extent to which their findings / conclusions matched what they expected to find. The mean mark for responses to this question was just 3 out of the 6 marks available, with nearly two-thirds of students scoring Level 1. Less successful responses were unable to make the link between conclusions and geographical ideas. Higher-level responses to this question were able to make that link with the best considering the extent to which their conclusions matched their expectations. Successful students had a good grasp of the outcomes of the fieldwork and the extent to which their conclusion was what they expected. They were able to articulate their conclusions linked to the fieldwork location, referring to specific results, suggesting how this matched their aim and ideas.

erText: In general, there appeared to be an improved understanding of the structure of their own fieldwork among students, compared to relatively recent years. Most students were able to articulate a clear aim that was rooted in a specific location. In recent series there has been a more obvious grasp of the different elements that make up a geographical investigation and how they are linked. However, in 2025 they performed less successfully than in 2024, particularly on question 2.5, where they were less secure on the planning of fieldwork and how this linked to outcomes. Some students found this question to be quite challenging and this may be because many were not involved in planning the fieldwork. It is important for centres to involve students in all stages of the fieldwork and to reflect on the whole process in terms of evaluating its success. Planning encompasses many aspects of what is done to prepare for fieldwork. Students considered a broad range of planning research in the answers, for example background reading, risk assessment and pilot studies. Over 80% of students achieved at least Level 2 but only around 10% achieved Level 3. To attain these higher marks, students must include specific details about their fieldwork and evaluate, in this case by considering the extent to which effective planning to generate successful outcomes. Too many students wrote about their fieldwork in a very generic manner, so it was difficult to ascertain where it took place or the specifics of what was done. Many students also stated that their fieldwork was 100% successful and whilst this may be possible, given the nature of variability in fieldwork, this is unlikely. The most successful responses talked about how planning led to a successful outcome but couldn’t account for the exact situation on the day. For example, some students talked about how they used OS maps to plan pedestrian accounts but in hindsight they should have used land-use maps as well, as they were unable to tell whether it was retail and this had an impact on results. Students should also be encouraged to use specific results in their responses as this aids clarity and depth.

text:
A group of students carried out an investigation to compare the number of shoppers
in the town centre of two small towns.
Town A has chain stores in an indoor shopping area.
Town B has an outdoor market area and has experienced regeneration focused on
the promotion of small, local and independent shops.
The students’ initial observation was that the number of shoppers was concentrated
in the indoor shopping area in Town A.  The number of shoppers fell steeply with
increased distance from the indoor centre.  In Town B, the students observed a
more even distribution of shoppers throughout the whole of the town centre.
Figure 3 outlines the relevant theory, the hypothesis and the sub-hypotheses.
Figure 3
Theory
Indoor shopping centres dominated by chain stores are part of the town centre of
many towns and cities.  These indoor shopping centres attract large numbers of
shoppers whilst smaller, independent shops outside of this enclosed shopping area
experience a much lower number of shoppers.
However, in recent years, as part of an attempt to regenerate town centres, there
has been more focus on promoting smaller, independent shops in open spaces.
This is likely to lead to a more even spread of shoppers across the town centre.
Hypothesis
The presence of an indoor shopping centre influences the distribution of shoppers
in a town centre.
Sub-hypotheses
In Town A, the number of shoppers will decrease significantly with distance from
the indoor shopping centre.
In Town B, there will be a more even distribution of shoppers in the town centre.

a central point in the town centre.  They used an OS map to determine 10 sampling
points.  They counted the number of pedestrians for 10 minutes at each point on
one morning.
They recorded the number of pedestrians passing each point using a tally chart
while timing on a mobile phone.  The students started at the central point and then
moved on to the other sites in turn.

erText: In Section C it was pleasing to note that most students were able to use the resources effectively, referring to the resources in their responses. text:
A group of students carried out an investigation to examine sorting of pebbles on a
beach at two locations.
The students wanted to compare pebble sorting on a beach backed by a sea wall to
one where no coastal protection schemes were in operation.
The students observed that where a sea wall was absent, beach pebbles appeared
to be more sorted than those where the beach was backed by a sea wall.
Figure 7 outlines the relevant theory, the hypothesis and the sub-hypotheses.
Figure 7
Theory
Pebble sorting is where beach material increases in size from the low tide mark
towards the back of the beach.
This happens when incoming waves carry larger material towards the back of the
beach and the power of returning seawater is weakened by infiltration, so only
smaller pebbles can be moved back towards the sea.  Therefore the pebble sizes
increase towards the back of the beach.
The students wanted to investigate if the presence of a sea wall would alter the
sorting of pebbles, as it may interfere with the movement of pebbles by wave
action, leading to a more even spread of pebble sizes across the beach.
Hypothesis
The beach without a sea wall will have more significant sorting of pebbles than the
beach with a sea wall.
Sub-hypotheses
The pebble size on the beach with no sea wall will increase with distance from the
low tide mark.
There will be a more even spread of pebble size across the beach with a sea wall.
Figure 8 outlines the students’ plan for primary data collection.
Figure 8
The students sampled pebbles every 10 metres along a line from the low tide mark
towards the high tide mark.  At each 10-metre interval, a pebble was measured
along its length.  To record the size, a pebble touching the foot of the student at the
sampling point was selected and measured using a ruler.

Notes for answers
• This is the area of land drained by a major river and its tributaries (1).

up within that one single river system (1).

erText: These questions assess how students interpret, analyse and evaluate data, evidence and resources. In general, analysis and interpretation of map evidence requires further development. Question 01.2, 04.2 and 06.2 were very accessible. Students coped with these graphically based questions, identifying patterns, manipulating data and picking out anomalies in support. In Question 01.2 (AO3) (6 marks) it’s evident that students are now well used to working with data, interpreting map information and analysis using data to support. The key to success was in understanding that this was a compound, cumulative bar graph showing how global emissions are predicted to fall by 2030. There was plenty to analyse here including the identification of Turkey and Mexico as obvious anomalies. Whilst there is never any credit for applying knowledge, this question did allow students to note that generally richer more developing counties were forecast to make bigger contributions to the reduction in greenhouse gases. This was because such information was hinted at in the resources through reference to G20 and non-G20 countries. This response is brief, but purposeful, picking out lots of key information showing a solid understanding of what the resource showed. Level 2 (6 marks)

Mark scheme

Notes for answers
AO1
• Drainage basins as open systems – inputs and outputs, to include
precipitation, evapo-transpiration and runoff; stores and flows, to
include interception, surface, soil water, groundwater and channel
storage; stemflow, infiltration overland flow, and channel flow.
Concept of water balance.
• Changes in the water cycle over time to include natural variation
including storm events, seasonal changes and human impact including
farming practices, land use change and water abstraction.
• Case study of a river catchment(s) at a local scale to illustrate and
analyse the key themes above, engage with field data and consider
the impact of precipitation upon drainage basin stores and transfers.
AO2
• The question is about the extent to which human and physical factors
(hinted at in the resource) help to achieve the definition of sustainable
water supply as set out in the note.
• Precipitation is the single most important physical factor in achieving a
sustainable water supply.  Without this, supply is unlikely to meet
demand.
• Similarly rates of evaporation will impact supplies of water.  For
example, high rates of evaporation in an area relying on lakes and
reservoirs, would point towards an unsustainable supply.
• Some may reference the importance of groundwater supply and
abstraction from rivers and lakes as important factors in the supply of
water.  The abstraction itself is clearly a human factor but the presence
of groundwater and sustainable supplies from rivers and lakes are
physical factors.  This itself is related to the permeability of the
underlying rock in the drainage basin.
• Wastewater treatment is clearly a human factor.  This points towards a
sustainable supply based on human intervention.
• Some may provide comparative information from case studies.
• In terms of relative importance, candidates are free to argue either
position as long as this is based on preceding content.

In question 01.3 (AO1 & AO2) (6 marks) there was no real credit for long narrative on either sustainable water supply case study material or on a flooding case study. This was not the focus of the question. Students had to pick out physical and human factors affecting the water cycle, many of which were hinted at in the resource. Once they did this, the question then needed some consideration of the relative importance i.e. which group of factors was more important in meeting the definition provided in the resource. Students were free to argue either way. Some suggested that without a supply of water in the first place, sustainability would be impossible to achieve. Others argued that it does not matter how much water is available, if it is not potable water, it can never be sustainable. This response produced a well-focused answer on the physical and human factors affecting the water cycle. It argued in favour that it does not matter how much water is available, if it is not potable water, it can never be sustainable and scored full marks. Level 2 (6 marks)
