erText: Question 04.5 had a mean score of over 12 and showed students had some clear knowledge and understanding of the possible impact of the changing carbon cycle on migration. Connections were drawn between increased carbon in the atmosphere, climate change, increased weather and climate related hazards, rising sea levels, impacts on agriculture, urban flooding and the possibility of climate related migration. There was evidence of good place knowledge here. Many focused on Pacific Island communities or sub-Saharan Africa. The 20-mark question in Section C required students to make synoptic links between physical and human themes and required students to make a connection between impacts of the changing carbon cycle taken from the physical geography core theme of water and carbon cycles, and an aspect of the human options. Questions 03.5, 04.5 and 05.5 all achieved mean marks within level 3. The synoptic question appears once each series in either Paper 1 or Paper 2 and makes links across specification content. In the 2025 series, the synoptic question appeared in the 20-mark questions in Section C for Paper 2. Depending on the optional topic studied, students were required to link aspects of the changing carbon cycle to one of the following themes: • Contemporary urban environments – managing environmental problems in urban areas. • Population and the environment – causes of migration. • Resource security – management of energy supply and/or consumption. The more successful responses to this question showed knowledge and understanding of changes within the carbon cycle, for example, such as increased atmospheric CO₂ resulting from fossil fuel combustion, leading to climate change and rising sea level. These changes were connected to the key aspect of the optional topic studied in each question with an evaluation of the question statement. Good responses made effective use of case studies to illustrate points made. Typically, they would have a clear structure and an evaluative conclusion. Some of the less successful responses to the synoptic question were not well-balanced in terms of the content from both areas of the specification. Some lack focus and there is a skill in crafting relatively concise answers that deal with the question directly whilst still showing some depth of knowledge and understanding. Student responses to the extended questions (20 marks) were often well structured and presented clear arguments with effective links to case studies. The 20-mark essays did highlight some areas for improvement. When answering 20-mark questions, students were more successful when the response continued with a single line of reasoning, compared to responses that try to offer a balanced argument or approach from different angles. This response links the impacts of changes to the carbon cycle to causes of migration. It has an assertive opening statement in the introduction. The response then goes on to make links between climate change, rising sea levels and migration from low lying and coastal communities such as The Netherlands. It connects changing rainfall patterns to possible impacts on agriculture and the consequences regarding migration. The student does offer an alternative perspective, which is not necessary, but credited. They show good synoptic thinking by integrating geographical theory into the response before finishing with a clear conclusion. This was also assessed as a Level 4 response as it is detailed with highly relevant and appropriate knowledge. It was given 20 marks. The response to question 04.5 shown below starts with an opinion (AO2), but the introduction is not particularly clear in terms of where the answer is going. There is some knowledge and understanding of the changing carbon budget and links to migration however there is no particular place focus. It refers to the impact on changing climate on agriculture and the links to migration, but apart from a reference to less developed countries there are no examples used. It finishes with a conclusion that rounds off the response. Overall, this was assessed as Level 2 and awarded 7 marks.

erText: Performance on the 4-mark questions assessing AO1 was a particular strength. The key to good marks in the 4-mark, AO1, questions is to make clear, focused responses that directly relate to the part of the specification being assessed. Specific knowledge is vital, and responses should be clear and if appropriate relate to a suitable example. Lower scoring responses to the 4-mark questions tend to show limited knowledge and understanding of the concept being assessed. Responses may make incorrect statements or simply not know enough about the topic. For those students studying Resource Security a number were unable to differentiate clearly between primary and secondary sources of energy.

erText: AO3 questions provide students with the opportunity to apply geographical skills of analysis and interpretation to a variety of resources presenting geographical information. Many students accessed Level 2 by demonstrating analytical skills such as identifying overall patterns and trends, data manipulation, picking out anomalies, making connections between resources, and accurately interpreting scales and legends. In general, there were some errors made by students on the resources questions (AO3). The resources from the skills checklist used to present geographical information in this paper included bar graphs (simple, compound and comparative, using both linear and logarithmic scales), maps and comparative line graphs. To score well in the skills questions students should aim to apply relevant skills directly to the data provided. These skills may include identifying overall patterns (‘the big picture’), recognising trends within the data, accurately reading scales and interpreting values, exemplifying key points and reporting on anomalies and manipulating data further to add depth to their analysis. Less successful responses to these questions can have a somewhat disjointed feel to them, lacking a clear sense of the bigger picture. They may also contain errors due to reading the data incorrectly. In question 05.2, many students understood the logarithmic horizontal scale; however, some did not, and as a result, their analysis was incorrect and limited to Level 1.

Notes for answers
The question requires an understanding of sustainability issues
associated with water supply.  Figures 10a and 10b present information
relating to the management of, and issues associated with wastewater.
Candidates should apply their knowledge of sustainable water
management, to assess how wastewater is a challenge to sustainable
water supply.  Candidates can also gain AO1 credit for reference to other
challenges for sustainable water supply.
AO1
• Sustainability issues associated with water management: virtual water
trade, conservation, recycling, ‘greywater’ and groundwater
management.
• Strategies to increase water supply to include catchment, diversion,
storage and water transfers and desalination.
• Strategies to manage water consumption (including reducing demand).
• Sources of water; components of demand, water stress.
AO2
•  Assessment using Figure 10a will probably come to the view that
there is very significance difference in the volumes of wastewater
produced, and more importantly in the amount that is treated and
recycled in different groups of countries.  Assessment of how this
highlights the huge missed potential for increased recycling of water
and hence more sustainable water supply.

small amounts of water that are currently recycled.  With HICs only
recycling, and therefore reusing less than 1/7 of the wastewater they
produce there is clearly significant unsustainability in the use of water.
Increased recycling of wastewater could improve the sustainability of
supply.
• Assessment of the information in Figure 10a may come to the view
that improving the sustainability of water supply through the increased
recycling of wastewater is a significant challenge.  At present only a
tiny minority of wastewater is recycled, especially in MICs and LICs,
where it may be the case that the need for improved water supply is
greatest.  Assessment may suggest that this implies there are
preventing increased use of recycling – for example, cost, availability
of resources, political will, or other priorities.

erText: In the 6- and 9-mark questions (AO1 & AO2) that used novel stimulus material there was evidence of some student confidence and clear application of knowledge and understanding. Most of the 6- and 9-mark questions evidenced some good subject knowledge and application. However, students could achieve higher marks within Level 2 or 3 by making their assessments and evaluations more explicit. These questions are based on the novel resources, designed to assess students’ abilities in how well they can apply their understanding of the specification topic to unfamiliar scenarios. Students should integrate their own knowledge and understanding, with the information presented in the novel material to answer the question. In both of the 6- and 9-mark questions, AO2 has a greater bearing on the distribution of marks, so the assessment or evaluation is more significant. Students should use their ‘own knowledge’ (AO1) to support their reasons. Students obtaining Level 1 in these questions often do not address the question posed or lean towards a description of the novel resources. In Section C, students chose to answer questions from the optional topics they had studied. o On question 03.3 the novel resource focussed on fortress developments o On question 04.3 the novel resource focused on female education and fertility o On question 05.3 the novel resources focused on wastewater and greywater management Students linked the resources to their own knowledge, rather than describing the information presented. In Section C, each of the 9-mark questions showed mean scores of over 5.0, indicating mid-level 2 performance. Students showed knowledge and evaluation of sustainable cities, local-scale factors negatively impacting health, and the geopolitics of mineral resources.

erText: The 20-mark question in Section C required students to make synoptic links between physical and human themes and required students to make a connection between impacts of the changing carbon cycle taken from the physical geography core theme of water and carbon cycles, and an aspect of the human options. Questions 03.5, 04.5 and 05.5 all achieved mean marks within level 3. The synoptic question appears once each series in either Paper 1 or Paper 2 and makes links across specification content. In the 2025 series, the synoptic question appeared in the 20-mark questions in Section C for Paper 2. Depending on the optional topic studied, students were required to link aspects of the changing carbon cycle to one of the following themes: • Contemporary urban environments – managing environmental problems in urban areas. • Population and the environment – causes of migration. • Resource security – management of energy supply and/or consumption. The more successful responses to this question showed knowledge and understanding of changes within the carbon cycle, for example, such as increased atmospheric CO₂ resulting from fossil fuel combustion, leading to climate change and rising sea level. These changes were connected to the key aspect of the optional topic studied in each question with an evaluation of the question statement. Good responses made effective use of case studies to illustrate points made. Typically, they would have a clear structure and an evaluative conclusion. Some of the less successful responses to the synoptic question were not well-balanced in terms of the content from both areas of the specification. Some lack focus and there is a skill in crafting relatively concise answers that deal with the question directly whilst still showing some depth of knowledge and understanding. Student responses to the extended questions (20 marks) were often well structured and presented clear arguments with effective links to case studies. The 20-mark essays did highlight some areas for improvement. When answering 20-mark questions, students were more successful when the response continued with a single line of reasoning, compared to responses that try to offer a balanced argument or approach from different angles. Question 05.5 required students to consider the extent to which impacts of changes to the carbon cycle will cause significant challenges for the management of energy supply and/or energy consumption. This example was credited at mid-Level 3 and awarded 13 marks. It begins by outlining changes to the carbon cycle linked to the enhanced greenhouse effect. It then goes on to explain how global warming will cause significant challenges to energy consumption with a focus on the demand for air conditioning in Saudi Arabia. It has some precise use of facts and figures in support (AO1). The second part of the answer linked to Nigeria is not fully relevant but there are some links to energy supply.
